summary: Discusses how Host Identity Protocol communication works across middleboxes, such as NATs and firewalls. Some middleboxes do not interfere, but others affect HIP or even block it. The document covers problems and how they may be handled. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Gates along the road can slow down or block travelers. This paper explains how a special kind of traveler, HIP, deals with different gates.

questions: what is hip host identity protocol
why does hip not work through nat
subtitle: Why NATs and firewalls get in the way of the Host Identity Protocol, and what could be done about it.

tldr.problem: The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) assumes simple Internet paths, but NATs and firewalls sit on many real paths and can block either its handshake or the encrypted data that follows.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through both phases of HIP (the base exchange and the ESP data exchange) for NATs and for firewalls, then outlines fixes: UDP encapsulation, rendezvous points, SPI-aware NATs and signaling to middleboxes.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem description, not a standard. It is an IRTF Research Group product, not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, and it leaves several choices open for further study.

today: RFC 5207 is an Informational IRTF document, not a candidate for any Internet Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains a problem statement rather than a protocol.

sections.title: Introduction: HIP Meets Middleboxes
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) specification, RFC 4423, assumes simple Internet paths where routers forward packets based on the destination address alone. That is increasingly rare. Middleboxes are devices that do more than a normal IP router, and RFC 3234 gave them that name.

NATs and firewalls are the most frequent middleboxes HIP traffic meets, so this memo covers only those. They can cause two kinds of trouble: interfering with HIP control traffic, or interfering with the HIP data traffic carried in the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

The document serves mainly as a problem description that solution proposals can reference. It also discusses known approaches and gives recommendations for some scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: HIP wants a clear road between two computers, but the road often has checkpoints in the middle. NATs and firewalls are the checkpoints this paper worries about.

sections.title: HIP Across NATs
sections.content:
HIP works in two phases: a base exchange handshake first, then application data. With IPv4 the base exchange rides in a new IP payload type. A basic NAT that only changes IP addresses can pass it. But basic NATs are rare, and NAPT devices that translate port numbers cannot relay it, because that payload has no port numbers or other demultiplexing fields.

A second issue is the well-known data receiver behind a NAT problem: a HIP node behind a NAT is not reachable unless it starts the communication, since the NAT holds no translation state for it.

With IPv6 the base exchange uses empty IPv6 packets with new HIP extension headers. IPv6 NATs are rare, but when they exist they will likely block IP payloads other than the well-known transport protocols, which includes this exchange.

In phase 2, HIP uses ESP, so it shares the NAT problems of IPsec described in RFC 3715. HIP hosts already avoid broken upper-layer checksums by using Host Identity Tags (HITs) instead of IP addresses in checksum calculations. The remaining trouble is the Security Parameter Index (SPI): a NAT can only see the SPIs of outgoing flows and cannot learn the SPIs of the return traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT is like a receptionist who only forwards mail with a proper room number. HIP's first letters have no room number, and a visitor can only get mail back if they wrote first.

sections.title: HIP Across Firewalls
sections.content:
Firewalls and packet filters inspect individual packets and decide to forward, drop or otherwise process them using filter rules. They are not inherently a problem for HIP, as long as the rules permit the HIP base exchange and IPsec traffic.

The trouble is that a common, recommended IPv4 configuration blocks all unknown traffic by default and allows only well-known transport protocols, so it blocks the base exchange. IPv6 firewalls are expected to block extension headers, or at least unknown ones, and payloads other than well-known transports, with the same result.

Firewalls also block traffic into the protected network that is not return traffic of an earlier outbound communication. That makes HIP peers unreachable from outside, much like the NAT case.

For phase 2, firewalls are less problematic than NATs. The largest concern is configurations that block ESP, because it is not a well-known transport protocol and ports cannot identify return flows. Firewalls could use mechanisms like SPI multiplexed NAT (SPINAT) to use SPIs as flow identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall is a strict guard who only lets in people on his list and anyone replying to someone inside. HIP's first message looks unfamiliar, so the guard stops it.

sections.title: Proposed Fixes: HIP and NAT Extensions
sections.content:
The memo suggests changes to HIP itself. UDP encapsulation may help with NATs and firewalls, and also with other middleboxes such as load balancers that use IP and transport-layer information. HIP nodes behind a NAT would tell their peers their contact information, the NAT's public IP address and a specific UDP port number, which would need a new HIP mechanism.

A rendezvous point lets nodes behind a NAT register an address and port where they can be contacted. Depending on the NAT type, it may be needed only during the base exchange or for the whole communication. It also helps nodes behind firewalls. The mobility management exchange of RFC 5206 could support this.

For the SPI problem, two methods exist. NATs can watch the base exchange and learn the agreed SPIs (SPINAT, which firewalls can use too but which needs HIP-specific NAT changes). Or peers can use a generic NAT or firewall signaling protocol to tell middleboxes the SPIs, which needs no HIP-specific middlebox changes. Candidates are the NSIS NATFW NSLP and the MIDCOM MIB module (RFC 5190). MIDCOM needs extra topology knowledge, which can be problematic in multihomed networks. NATFW NSLP reaches all NATs and firewalls on the path and has a proxy mode for when only one end supports NSIS.
sections.plainLanguage: One fix is to wrap HIP letters in an envelope the gatekeepers already know. Another is a meeting spot where hidden computers leave their address, and a third is telling the gatekeepers ahead of time what to expect.

sections.title: Legacy NATs, Firewalls and Other Middleboxes
sections.content:
The fixes above need NATs and firewalls to be updated, but upgrading or replacing all deployed devices is impossible. For legacy devices the memo focuses on IPv4, since most deployed NATs support only IPv4.

UDP encapsulation solves some problems: UDP packets usually cross NATs and firewalls when the communication starts from the inside, though traffic started outside is typically dropped. ESP still causes trouble even then. Some NATs offer VPN pass-through, which tries to correlate outgoing and incoming SPIs, but this often works reliably only for a small number of nodes behind a single NAT because of SPI collisions.

A better option may be UDP encapsulation for ESP (RFC 3948), enabled through a new parameter in the base exchange. Whether to mandate UDP encapsulation for all HIP traffic is left for further study. UPnP is also mentioned as a way to configure middleboxes on the same link as a HIP node.

Other middlebox types are not covered; future versions of the document may describe them.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every old gatekeeper can be retrained, so HIP may have to dress its letters up as ordinary UDP mail. That works for outgoing letters but still gets messy for the replies.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Opening pinholes in firewalls (loading rules that let packets through) and creating NAT bindings are highly security-sensitive actions. Any mechanism that does this to support HIP traversal should be well protected. The memo points to the security sections of RFC 3715 and RFC 5190 for details.

The document admits that it has not considered whether some of the listed options pose additional threats to the security of HIP itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking a guard to open a gate is risky, so whoever asks must prove they are allowed. The authors have not yet checked every idea for new dangers.

viz.caption: WHERE EACH MIDDLEBOX HURTS HIP (SUMMARY OF RFC 5207)

cells: NAPTs cannot relay a payload with no port numbers
Default-deny rules block the unknown payload
Likely blocks payloads other than well-known transports
Extension headers and unknown payloads likely blocked
Often blocks ESP; SPINAT-like flow IDs possible
